::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation statistics estimator exponential" data-difficulty="0" #q-concepts-estimator-estimate}
## Model, parameter, estimator, and estimate

Waiting times $X_1,\ldots,X_4$ are modelled as i.i.d. Exponential random
variables with unknown rate $\lambda>0$, so
$$
f(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x>0,
\qquad \mathrm{E}[X_i]=1/\lambda.
$$
The observed waiting times, in minutes, are $0.5$, $1$, $1.5$, and $3$.

(a) Identify the parameter and its parameter space. What does i.i.d. assume?  
(b) Calculate $\bar x$ and the observed value of the rate estimator
$\hat\lambda=4/\sum_i X_i$. State the units of each.  
(c) Which of $\bar X$, $4/\sum_i X_i$, and $\bar X-1/\lambda$ are statistics?
Explain the distinction between an estimator and an estimate.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The parameter is the rate $\lambda$, with parameter space $(0,\infty)$.
The i.i.d. assumption says the waiting times are mutually independent and
all have the same Exponential distribution, including the same rate.

**(b)** The observed total is $6$ minutes, giving
$$
\bar x=\frac64=1.5\text{ minutes},\qquad
\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac46=\frac23\text{ per minute}.
$$
The mean waiting time and the rate are different targets, with reciprocal units.

**(c)** Both $\bar X$ and $4/\sum_i X_i$ are statistics: their values can be
computed from the observations without knowing the parameter. The quantity
$\bar X-1/\lambda$ is not a statistic because it depends on the unknown rate.
An estimator is a statistic used to estimate a target; it is random before
sampling. Its realised numerical value, such as $2/3$ per minute, is an estimate.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation estimator bias variance mse consistency normal" data-difficulty="1" #q-concepts-unbiased-consistent}
## Unbiased and consistent are different properties

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\sigma^2>0$.
Consider two estimators of $\mu$:
$$
T_n=X_1,\qquad U_n=\bar X+\frac1n.
$$

(a) Find the bias and variance of each estimator.  
(b) Show directly that $T_n$ is not consistent by considering
$\mathrm{Pr}(|T_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)$ for a fixed $\varepsilon>0$.  
(c) Use the sufficient condition based on bias and variance to show that
$U_n$ is consistent. What do these examples show about unbiasedness?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** For every $n$,
$$
\mathrm{Bias}(T_n)=0,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(T_n)=\sigma^2,
$$
whereas
$$
\mathrm{Bias}(U_n)=\frac1n,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(U_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$
Adding a constant changes the mean but not the variance.

**(b)** The distribution of $T_n$ does not change with $n$:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(|T_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)
=2\left[1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\right)\right]>0.
$$
This fixed positive probability cannot tend to zero, so $T_n$ is not
consistent. It ignores every observation after the first. Merely failing a
sufficient condition would not prove inconsistency; this calculation does.

**(c)** Both the bias $1/n$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$ tend to zero, so $U_n$
is consistent. Equivalently,
$$
\mathrm{MSE}(U_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\frac1{n^2}\longrightarrow0.
$$
Thus an unbiased estimator need not be consistent, and an estimator can be
biased at every finite sample size yet still be consistent. Unbiasedness
concerns the mean at a given sample size; consistency concerns concentration
around the target as the sample size grows.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation likelihood bernoulli bayes" data-difficulty="1" #q-concepts-likelihood-probability}
## Likelihood is not a posterior probability

Four conditionally independent Bernoulli trials produce the ordered outcomes
$(1,1,1,0)$. The common success probability $\theta$ can take only the values
$1/4$ and $3/4$.

(a) Calculate the likelihood at each possible parameter value and their ratio.  
(b) A student says: “The larger likelihood is the probability that
$\theta=3/4$.” Explain the error.  
(c) Now assign prior probabilities $\mathrm{Pr}(\theta=1/4)=0.8$ and
$\mathrm{Pr}(\theta=3/4)=0.2$. Find the posterior probability of $\theta=3/4$.  
(d) If only the total number of successes had been recorded, how would the
likelihoods and the answer to part (c) change?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** For this ordered sequence the likelihood is $L(\theta)=\theta^3(1-\theta)$:
$$
L(1/4)=\frac3{256},\qquad L(3/4)=\frac{27}{256},\qquad
\frac{L(3/4)}{L(1/4)}=9.
$$
The observed sequence is nine times as probable under $\theta=3/4$ as under
$\theta=1/4$.

**(b)** Each likelihood is the probability of the observed data **given** a
parameter value. It is not the probability of that parameter **given** the
data. Likelihood values need not sum to one over parameter values. A Bayesian
posterior requires a prior and normalisation.

**(c)** Multiply by the prior weights and normalise:
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(\theta=3/4\mid\underline x)
=\frac{(27/256)(0.2)}{(3/256)(0.8)+(27/256)(0.2)}
=\frac9{13}\approx0.6923.
$$
Normalising the likelihoods alone would give $0.9$, which would correspond
to equal prior probabilities, not the prior specified here.

**(d)** The count has a $\mathrm{Binomial}(4,\theta)$ distribution. Both
likelihoods acquire the same factor $\binom43=4$, becoming $3/64$ and $27/64$.
That factor cancels from the ratio and from the posterior, so part (c) is
unchanged. The probability of a count differs from that of one ordered sequence.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation confidence-interval hypothesis-test normal clt z-test t-test" data-difficulty="0" #q-concepts-choose-method}
## Choosing a method from the assumptions

In each scenario below, the observations form an i.i.d. sample and the target
is the population mean $\mu$. For a confidence interval or a test of
$H_0:\mu=\mu_0$, choose an appropriate method and state whether its calibration
is exact or approximate. Give the statistic and reference distribution when
available.

(a) $n=12$ observations from a Normal population with known variance $\sigma^2$.  
(b) $n=12$ observations from a Normal population with unknown variance.  
(c) $n=200$ observations from a non-Normal population with finite, nonzero
variance.  
(d) $n=8$ observations from a strongly skewed population with unknown variance.
Is an exact Normal-theory $t$ procedure justified by the information given?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Use an exact Normal $z$ procedure. Under $H_0$,
$$
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$
Normality of the observations makes this exact even for $n=12$.

**(b)** Use an exact one-sample $t$ procedure. With the usual sample standard
deviation $S$, under $H_0$,
$$
T=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{11}.
$$
The degrees of freedom are $n-1$, and replacing $\sigma$ by $S$ introduces
uncertainty that the $t$ distribution accounts for.

**(c)** A CLT-based Normal procedure is a possible large-sample approximation:
$$
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}\overset{\mathrm{approx.}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1)
\quad\text{under }H_0.
$$
Its finite-sample accuracy depends on the population's shape, including its
tails. A sample size of $200$ does not guarantee a good approximation for
every finite-variance distribution.

**(d)** No. An exact $t$ distribution relies on the Normal sampling model,
and $n=8$ with strong skewness gives little support for a CLT approximation.
More information about the population model or a different justified method
is needed. Unknown variance alone does not make a $t$ procedure exact.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation confidence-interval credible-interval normal standard-error" data-difficulty="0" #q-concepts-interval-interpretation}
## What a 95% interval does and does not say

An i.i.d. Normal sample has known population standard deviation $\sigma=8$,
sample size $n=64$, and observed mean $\bar x=15$. Use $z_{0.975}=1.96$.

(a) Calculate a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$.  
(b) Explain what is correct or incorrect about each statement:

1. “This method produces intervals containing the true mean in $95\%$ of
   repeated samples under the model.”
2. “There is now a $95\%$ frequentist probability that $\mu$ lies between
   these two observed endpoints.”
3. “About $95\%$ of individual observations lie in this interval.”

(c) How would the interval's width change if the sample size increased to
$256$, with the same known population standard deviation and confidence level?  
(d) If a Bayesian analysis instead reported a $95\%$ credible interval, what
probability statement would that support?

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The standard error is $8/\sqrt{64}=1$, so the interval is
$$
15\pm1.96(1)=[13.04,16.96].
$$

**(b)** Statement 1 is the correct repeated-sampling interpretation (up to
rounding of the Normal quantile). Before sampling, the endpoints are random.
Statement 2 incorrectly assigns frequentist probability to a fixed parameter
lying in a now fixed interval; the realised interval either contains $\mu$
or it does not. Statement 3 confuses uncertainty about a mean with the spread
of observations. Individual observations have standard deviation $8$, whereas
the sample mean has standard error $1$.

**(c)** Width is proportional to $1/\sqrt n$. Increasing $n$ by a factor of
four halves the width from $3.92$ to $1.96$. It need not leave the centre
unchanged, because a new sample may have a different mean.

**(d)** For a credible interval $[l,u]$ one can write
$$
\mathrm{Pr}(l\le\mu\le u\mid\underline x)=0.95,
$$
with probability taken under the posterior distribution, conditional on the
data and the chosen prior and sampling model. A frequentist confidence
interval cannot be given that interpretation without a Bayesian analysis.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation hypothesis-test p-value z-test one-sided two-sided" data-difficulty="0" #q-concepts-p-values}
## The alternative determines the p-value

A test statistic for a Normal mean has an exact standard Normal distribution
under $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$. Its observed value is $z_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.80$.
You may use $\Phi(1.80)=0.9641$.

(a) Calculate the $p$-value for the pre-specified alternative $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$.  
(b) Calculate the $p$-value for the pre-specified alternative $H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$.  
(c) State the decision at the $5\%$ level in each case. Does either $p$-value
give the probability that $H_0$ is true?  
(d) Explain why choosing a one-sided alternative after seeing the sign of the
observed statistic is problematic.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** For the right-sided alternative, larger values are more extreme:
$$
p=\mathrm{Pr}_{H_0}(Z\ge1.80)=1-0.9641=0.0359.
$$

**(b)** For the two-sided alternative, both tails count:
$$
p=\mathrm{Pr}_{H_0}(|Z|\ge1.80)=2(1-0.9641)=0.0718.
$$

**(c)** Reject $H_0$ for the right-sided test since $0.0359<0.05$. Fail to
reject it for the two-sided test since $0.0718>0.05$. This latter decision
does not prove $\mu=\mu_0$. Each $p$-value is a tail probability for a statistic
**assuming the null model**, not a posterior probability of that model.

**(d)** The rejection rule must be specified before inspecting the outcome.
If we always choose the observed direction and use a $5\%$ one-sided cutoff,
we reject in either tail beyond $\pm z_{0.95}$. Under the continuous standard
Normal null this has probability $0.05+0.05=0.10$, not $0.05$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation hypothesis-test power normal z-test one-sided" data-difficulty="1" #q-concepts-power-errors}
## Type I error, Type II error, and power

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_{16}$ be i.i.d. $\mathcal N(\mu,64)$ observations. Test
$H_0:\mu=20$ against $H_1:\mu>20$ by rejecting when
$$
Z=\frac{\bar X-20}{8/\sqrt{16}}>1.645.
$$
For these calculations use $\Phi(1.645)\approx0.95$,
$\Phi(0.355)\approx0.6387$, and $\Phi(2.355)\approx0.9907$.

(a) Express the rejection region in terms of $\bar X$ and calculate the
Type I error probability.  
(b) If the true mean is $\mu=24$, find the power and Type II error probability.  
(c) Repeat the power calculation for $n=64$, using the same $5\%$ one-sided
test. Explain why the Type I error probability stays the same while power changes.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The standard error is $2$, so reject when
$\bar X>20+1.645(2)=23.29$. Under $H_0$, $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, giving
$$
\mathrm{Pr}_{\mu=20}(\text{reject }H_0)=1-\Phi(1.645)\approx0.05.
$$
A Type I error is rejecting when the null is true.

**(b)** Under $\mu=24$, $\bar X\sim\mathcal N(24,4)$, so
$$
\mathrm{Power}(24)=\mathrm{Pr}_{\mu=24}(\bar X>23.29)
=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{23.29-24}{2}\right)
=\Phi(0.355)\approx0.6387.
$$
The Type II error probability at $\mu=24$ is $1-0.6387=0.3613$:
failing to reject when this alternative value is true. Power is a function
of the true mean, not a single probability shared by all alternatives.

**(c)** With $n=64$ the standard error is $1$, so the rejection boundary becomes
$20+1.645=21.645$. At $\mu=24$,
$$
\mathrm{Power}(24)=1-\Phi(21.645-24)=\Phi(2.355)\approx0.9907.
$$
The null-standardised statistic is still standard Normal and uses the same
cutoff, maintaining size approximately $0.05$ (the approximation is only from
rounding the cutoff). The smaller standard error makes a mean of $24$ easier
to distinguish from $20$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation bayes conjugacy beta binomial map" data-difficulty="1" #q-concepts-sequential-bayes}
## Sequential Bayesian updating and prior influence

Conditional on a fixed success probability $p$, all trials below are independent
Bernoulli trials. Begin with the prior $p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,3)$. A first batch
contains $3$ successes in $5$ trials; a second batch contains $1$ success in
$3$ trials.

(a) Find the posterior after each batch, using the first posterior as the
prior for the second update.  
(b) Check that updating once with all the data gives the same final posterior.
Find its posterior mean and MAP estimate.  
(c) Express the final posterior mean as a weighted average of the original
prior mean and the overall observed success proportion.  
(d) Repeat the final posterior mean calculation for a
$\mathrm{Beta}(20,30)$ prior. Explain the effect of this change.

You may use that a $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ distribution has mean $a/(a+b)$ and,
when $a,b>1$, mode $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** A Beta update adds successes to the first shape parameter and failures
to the second. The first batch has $2$ failures, giving
$$
p\mid\text{batch 1}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2+3,3+2)=\mathrm{Beta}(5,5).
$$
The second batch has $2$ failures, so
$$
p\mid\text{both batches}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(5+1,5+2)=\mathrm{Beta}(6,7).
$$

**(b)** There are $4$ successes and $4$ failures overall. One update gives
$\mathrm{Beta}(2+4,3+4)=\mathrm{Beta}(6,7)$, as above. Conditional independence
lets us multiply the batch likelihoods in either order. The posterior summaries are
$$
\mathrm{E}[p\mid\underline x]=\frac6{13}\approx0.4615,\qquad
\hat p_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\frac5{11}\approx0.4545.
$$
The posterior mean and mode need not coincide.

**(c)** The original prior mean is $2/5=0.4$ and the sample proportion is
$4/8=0.5$. Thus
$$
\frac6{13}=\frac5{13}(0.4)+\frac8{13}(0.5).
$$
The weights are proportional to the prior shape sum $a+b$ and the number of
trials. The result lies between the prior mean and the observed proportion.

**(d)** The new prior has the same mean $0.4$ but is more concentrated. The
posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(24,34)$, with mean
$$
\frac{24}{58}=\frac{50}{58}(0.4)+\frac8{58}(0.5)
=\frac{12}{29}\approx0.4138.
$$
The larger prior weight keeps the posterior mean closer to $0.4$ for these
eight trials. This illustrates how prior concentration affects an update even
when the prior mean is unchanged.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="interpretation bayes credible-interval hdi beta cdf" data-difficulty="1" #q-concepts-credible-hdi}
## Equal-tailed and highest-density credible intervals

Suppose the posterior density of a parameter $\theta$ is
$$
\pi(\theta\mid\underline x)=2\theta,\qquad 0\le\theta\le1,
$$
and zero elsewhere.

(a) Find the posterior CDF and its quantile of order $p$, for $0<p<1$.  
(b) Find a $90\%$ equal-tailed credible interval.  
(c) Find a $90\%$ highest-density interval (HDI). Explain why its upper
endpoint is $1$.  
(d) Compare the intervals' lengths and state what they have in common.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** On the support,
$$
F(\theta\mid\underline x)=\int_0^\theta2t\,\mathrm{d}t=\theta^2.
$$
The CDF is zero below $0$ and one above $1$. Solving $q_p^2=p$ gives
$q_p=\sqrt p$.

**(b)** Leave $0.05$ posterior probability in each tail:
$$
[q_{0.05},q_{0.95}]=[\sqrt{0.05},\sqrt{0.95}]
\approx[0.2236,0.9747].
$$

**(c)** The density increases throughout the support. The highest-density
values therefore form an interval $[a,1]$. Requiring posterior mass $0.90$ gives
$$
\int_a^1 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta=1-a^2=0.90,
$$
so the HDI is $[\sqrt{0.10},1]\approx[0.3162,1]$. Every interior point of
this interval has higher density than points excluded below it. There is no
requirement for equal tail probabilities, or equal endpoint densities when
an endpoint is a boundary of the support.

**(d)** The equal-tailed interval has length approximately $0.7511$; the HDI
has length approximately $0.6838$. Both contain $90\%$ of the posterior
probability, but the HDI is shorter here because it uses the part of the support
with greatest density. Neither says that future observations fall in the
interval with probability $0.90$: these are intervals for the parameter.

</details>

:::
